analysis.investment_thesis: CEAT is a respectable second-tier tyre maker riding India's auto upcycle, but with a 9-year net profit CAGR of barely 0.9% and ROE stuck at 11.8%, it is not the compounder I look for. The forward P/E of 18x is fair but not a bargain given the thin margin and rising debt profile.
key_strengths: Revenue scaling well — INR 13,218 Cr in FY25 (+10.3% CAGR 9Y), riding OEM and replacement demand from India's two-wheeler and passenger car growth
EBITDA recovery to INR 1,513 Cr in FY25 after the FY22 raw-material trough, showing operating leverage in the business
OCF positive all 5 years; FY24 FCF of INR 852 Cr demonstrates the business can generate cash when input costs normalise
key_risks: Debt surged sharply — borrowings jumped from INR 1,792 Cr (FY24) to INR 3,114 Cr (FY25), D/E now 0.68x and finance costs compounding at 11.9% CAGR; leverage undermines profitability
Net profit fell from INR 635 Cr (FY24) to INR 471 Cr (FY25) despite revenue growth of 10.7% — margin erosion in rising-cost environment is the structural vulnerability
Intense competition from MRF, Apollo, and multinational brands limits pricing power; rubber and carbon black volatility creates unpredictable earnings swings
red_flags: Promoter holding at 47.21% — below the 50% threshold I like to see; signals limited skin-in-the-game
9-year net profit CAGR of just 0.9% despite a decade of India auto growth — capital deployed has not translated to shareholder wealth
FY25 FCF collapsed to INR 149 Cr vs INR 852 Cr in FY24, even as capex remained near INR 943 Cr — cash generation is inconsistent
analysis.detailed_analysis: CEAT benefits from India's structural auto demand — two-wheelers, tractors, and the OEM mix are solid long-term plays. But the tyre industry is a commodity-input, margin-thin business, and CEAT has consistently struggled to convert revenue growth into earnings growth; a 10% revenue CAGR producing a 0.9% PAT CAGR over nine years is deeply uninspiring for a long-term compounder. The FY25 spike in borrowings (INR 3,114 Cr vs INR 1,792 Cr prior year) and a corresponding collapse in FCF to INR 149 Cr raises questions about whether the ongoing capex cycle will generate adequate returns. ROCE of 15.4% is acceptable but trending in the wrong direction after heavy investment. For me, tyres are not a structural India growth story — they are a cyclical commodity play with periodic margin booms and busts, and CEAT does not have the moat or the management track record to deserve a premium rating.
